mz.headline: Evergreen Marine launches China-Maputo container service
mz.dek: New AEF5 route offers Gauteng importers an alternative to Durban, with a shorter rail link from Maputo.
paragraphs: Evergreen Marine will start a new container service connecting China to Mozambique's port of Maputo on November 25, 2026. The AEF5 service's first vessel departs Shanghai, with stops in Ningbo, Nansha, Port Klang, Dar es Salaam, and Maputo before returning via Singapore. This route provides Gauteng importers with a new option for shipments from China, aiming to bypass potential border delays.

The port of Maputo offers a rail distance of 584 kilometers to Johannesburg, shorter than Durban's 720 kilometers, according to World Bank data. However, the actual delivery time and cost depend on shipping schedules, inland transport charges, and customs clearance at the Ressano Garcia and Komatipoort border posts. Maputo Port Development Company aims for a terminal capacity of 530,000 TEUs.

The commercial benefit for Gauteng importers hinges on whether the total door-to-door transit time and cost from Maputo can compete with the Durban route. Evergreen has not yet announced the sailing frequency or available capacity for the AEF5 service. This new route complements Evergreen's existing SAF service, which already serves Durban and Cape Town.

mz.headline: Mozambique reports 154 terror attacks in five months
mz.dek: Insurgents targeted 16 districts in Cabo Delgado and Niassa provinces, affecting 120 communities.
paragraphs: More than 150 terrorist attacks occurred in northern Mozambique between June and October, with most incidents concentrated in Cabo Delgado province. Brigadier-General Sérgio Estrela, Commander of the EU Military Assistance Mission in Mozambique (EUMAM MOZ), presented these findings in Maputo, noting the geographic spread and mobility of insurgent groups. The attacks affected 16 districts, including 15 in Cabo Delgado and one in Niassa, impacting 120 localities.

Estrela highlighted that insurgent tactics now include kidnappings and ransom demands, making monitoring important for effective responses. Local communities report limited presence of Mozambican Defence Armed Forces (FADM) in areas of Muidumbe and Mueda, allowing insurgents greater freedom of movement. The Islamic State of Mozambique claimed responsibility on November 1 for killing 14 people in Muidumbe and Mueda districts the previous week.

An investigator from the Institute of Security Studies noted that despite nine years of external training and equipment efforts for the Mozambican armed forces, concrete results on the ground remain insufficient. Communities continue to suffer from inadequate security and human rights violations.

mz.headline: Mozambique plans Matola LNG terminal by 2027
mz.dek: A new liquefied natural gas terminal in Matola aims to secure energy supply as Pande and Temane gas fields decline.
paragraphs: Mozambique is preparing an alternative to the Pande and Temane gas production, which is expected to end in 2030. The country is advancing with a liquefied natural gas (GNL) terminal project in Matola, aiming for financial close by the end of 2027. The Beluluane Gas Company (BGC) announced the appointment of the VGI/PRDW consortium as Owner's Engineer for the terminal.

This appointment will help consolidate engineering projects and support the hiring of the contractor for the infrastructure's construction. The BGC stated this step is crucial for ensuring the supply of power to gas-fired plants in Chókwè, Ressano Garcia, and Maputo, which provide around 450 megawatts to Eletricidade de Moçambique (EDM). It will also supply the industrial sector in the Matola and Maputo regions.

The Pande and Temane fields, operated by Sasol, have produced 3,306.41 petajoules of gas up to October 2025. Sasol anticipates extraction will cease in 2030, though investments could extend operations to 2031. Commercial negotiations for GNL supply and financing for the Matola terminal are in their final stages, with further announcements expected soon.

na.headline: President intervenes to save N$41.1 billion Dangote investment
na.dek: Namibian president personally persuaded industrialist Aliko Dangote to continue with the project after his team faced bureaucratic delays.
paragraphs: President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah revealed on Wednesday, 4 November 2026, that Namibia nearly lost a N$41.1 billion investment from Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote due to government bureaucratic delays. The Dangote Namibia Tank Farm and Regional Pipeline Project, valued at US$2.5 billion, was at risk of being abandoned. President Nandi-Ndaitwah personally intervened by contacting Dangote to plead for patience and ensure the project proceeded.

The President stated she placed the project directly under the Office of the President, assigning National Planning Commission Director General Ambassador Kaire Mbuende to oversee its implementation. This action followed past experiences where similar projects, including a proposed shipyard, were lost after investors became frustrated with administrative obstacles over several years. The shipyard investors withdrew after four years of trying to establish their project.

Nandi-Ndaitwah expressed determination to prevent another investment loss, citing the urgent need for job creation and poverty reduction. She instructed relevant ministries and the National Planning Commission to work closely with Dangote Industries, declaring the project a "presidential project" until completion. This intervention aims to create an environment where investors are supported by efficient processes, rather than requiring presidential intervention.

na.headline: Namibia launches state air ambulance after patient deaths
na.dek: The new service uses a Learjet and helicopters to speed up emergency medical transfers.
paragraphs: Namibia launched its first state-owned air ambulance service in Windhoek on Wednesday, following the deaths of patients who could not reach specialized hospitals in time. Health minister Esperance Luvindao said the service aims to reduce travel time for critically ill and injured patients, especially in remote areas.

Luvindao recounted the loss of a 12-year-old boy from Katima Mulilo and other patients after an April 2026 road accident near Otjiwarongo as key motivators. Vice President Lucia Witbooi stated the service ensures survival is not determined by location, addressing challenges from Namibia's vast geography.

The service includes a Learjet equipped for critical care, with Government Air Transport Services providing aircraft and pilots. Helicopter evacuations will also be available through cooperation with the Namibian Police and Defence Forces, ensuring specialized medical personnel accompany patients to national referral hospitals.

na.headline: Namibia to send teachers to The Bahamas
na.dek: The two nations will deepen educational cooperation, addressing a shortage of maths and science educators.
paragraphs: Namibia has signalled its willingness to assist The Bahamas with deploying qualified Namibian educators. The deployment will address The Bahamas’ deficit of teachers in mathematics, science, and technical vocational subjects. This initiative underscores deepening bilateral cooperation in education between the two countries.

Prime Minister Elijah Ngurare and his Bahamian counterpart Philip Davis discussed the teacher deployment on the sidelines of the 2026 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda. Ngurare assured that Namibia will evaluate the manpower request through local State institutions, balancing The Bahamas’ needs with Namibia’s staffing requirements and professional standards.

The leaders also discussed expanding trade and investment, with Namibia identifying beef, grapes, blueberries, and dates for export to the Caribbean. A Bahamian trade and investment mission, led by Prime Minister Davis, is scheduled for March 2027 to finalise commercial partnerships.

na.headline: AI could add N$3.58 billion to Namibia's economy
na.dek: A new study ranks Namibia 36th out of 56 Commonwealth nations in AI readiness, citing infrastructure and youth unemployment.
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence could boost Namibia's economy by N$3.58 billion over the next decade, according to a 2026 Commonwealth Youth AI Readiness Index study. The Ayre Think Tank report estimates potential GDP gains between N$1.73 billion and N$5.43 billion, with a moderate scenario projecting N$3.58 billion. This study was released on Thursday during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.

The report places Namibia 36th among 56 Commonwealth countries, scoring 42.7 out of 100, below the study's benchmark of 53. High youth unemployment, with 47% of young people in the labour force jobless, and limited electricity access reaching 59.3% of the population, are identified as major challenges. Inadequate digital infrastructure, including slow broadband and internet disruptions, further restricts the country's ability to benefit from AI.

Namibia has approximately 800,000 young people aged 15 to 29 who could benefit from AI-related opportunities. However, the index gave Namibia a low score of 3.1 out of 10 for decent work, enterprise, and transitions. Researchers noted gaps in digital education, with computing not recorded in the curriculum, and insufficient comparable evidence of digital and AI skills among young Namibians.

na.headline: Namibian woman accused of murder to remain in custody
na.dek: Nambwa Matengu, 38, faces charges of murder, attempted murder, and arson after a fatal fire in Katima Mulilo.
paragraphs: Katima Mulilo resident Nambwa Matengu, 38, will spend Christmas in custody after appearing in court on Thursday, accused of setting her flatmate's room ablaze in August. Nsala Mwazi, 42, died in the fire while trying to push her two daughters to safety through burglar windows. The state alleges Matengu used petrol to start the fire at approximately 00:34 on August 24 in the Shackdweller location, blocking Mwazi's escape route from the outside.

Matengu faces charges of murder, two counts of attempted murder, and arson. She informed the court she is awaiting a state legal aid lawyer. State prosecutor Cedric Mundia opposed bail, citing ongoing investigations and public interest. Magistrate Davy Kambinda postponed the case to February 8 for the accused to receive legal representation and for investigations to proceed.

Family and friends of the deceased gathered at the court to protest any possibility of Matengu being released on bail. Matengu has been in custody since her arrest. The court heard that the police found a 5-liter container smelling of petrol near Mwazi's bedroom door.

ne.headline: Niger police dismantle fake medical aid scam
ne.dek: A trader confessed to fabricating distress stories and using his child's photo to solicit funds.
paragraphs: Niger's Judicial Police Directorate announced on November 5, 2026, the dismantling of a scam network that used fake medical aid appeals on social media. The network solicited financial contributions from citizens by exploiting their compassion. The police received a complaint on March 1, 2026, from the General Referral Hospital (HGR) in Niamey about an individual posting alarming messages seeking public financial aid for supposed gravely ill patients.

The investigation identified the account holder and revealed fraudulent activities began in January 2026. Fabricated cases included a 70-year-old woman needing FCFA 10,490,000 for evacuation to Ouagadougou, and an orphan, Abdourahamane, needing FCFA 1,637,000 for a lung infection. The suspect, a merchant with a master's degree in accounting, admitted to creating these stories and altering his own child's photo. He was apprehended with FCFA 548,624 and multiple SIM cards.

The police are urging mobile phone companies to strengthen subscriber identification to prevent fraudulent use of money transfer services. They also advise the public to verify aid appeals with health facilities before sending money.

ne.headline: Niger and Mali presidents discuss Sahel security
ne.dek: Presidents Tiani and Goïta reaffirmed commitment to the Sahel States Confederation and counter-terrorism efforts.
paragraphs: Niger's President Abdourahamane Tiani and Mali's President Assimi Goïta met in Niamey on Thursday, November 5, 2026, to discuss security challenges within the Sahel States Confederation (AES). The leaders held a private meeting followed by expanded talks involving their delegations, focusing on counter-terrorism and regional stability.

Niger's Foreign Minister Bakary Yaou Sangaré stated the visit aimed to strengthen ties between the two nations and review progress in defense, diplomacy, and development within the AES. Both presidents praised the unified force's successes against terrorism and coordinated diplomatic actions that bolster the Confederation's standing.

Discussions also covered socio-economic integration, including free movement of people and goods, transport infrastructure, agro-industrial development, and energy and mining resources. rw.headline: Mushikiwabo seeks third term leading Francophonie
rw.dek: Rwandan Louise Mushikiwabo is running for re-election as head of the international organisation on November 16.
paragraphs: Rwandan national Louise Mushikiwabo is seeking a third term as the leader of La Francophonie, with elections scheduled for November 16 in Phnom Penh. She faces competition from Juliana Amato Lumumba of Congo, Coumba Bâ of Mauritania, and Dacian Cioloș of Romania. Kinshasa has accused Kigali of aiding rebels, a claim Rwanda denies, while Kigali accuses Kinshasa of supporting FDLR rebels.

Mushikiwabo, who has led the organisation since 2018 and was re-elected in 2022, benefits from incumbency and familiarity with the organisation's mechanisms. French President Emmanuel Macron previously backed her candidacy, stating she has "all the skills for the job." Rwandan President Paul Kagame has actively lobbied African leaders and OIF member states to support her bid for re-election.

Congolese candidate Juliana Amato Lumumba's bid aims to leverage the DRC's demographic weight for institutional influence. Her candidacy raises questions about the Francophonie's focus on major demographic and cultural hubs. The DRC views its candidate's challenge as a stance against Rwanda, potentially complicating Lumumba's efforts to gain broader support beyond Kinshasa's allies.

rw.headline: Rwanda showcases dried fruits and chili at China expo
rw.dek: The nation aims to boost exports to China, which reached $227 million in 2025.
paragraphs: Rwanda is exhibiting coffee, tea, honey, chili, dried fruits, and macadamia nuts at the ninth China International Import Expo in Shanghai, which began on November 5 and runs until November 10. The country is using the six-day event to seek increased exports to the Chinese market and promote investment, tourism, and cultural exchange.

Rwanda’s Ambassador to China, Lt Gen (Rtd) Emmanuel Karenzi Karake, stated that the expo offers a significant platform for Rwandan businesses, including smallholder farmers and women-led cooperatives, to connect with Chinese consumers. This participation coincides with 55 years of diplomatic ties between Rwanda and China.

Bilateral trade between the two nations reached approximately $849 million in 2025, a substantial increase from $300 million in 2019. Rwandan exports to China alone grew by 549% from $35 million in 2019 to $227 million in 2025, while Chinese investment in Rwanda rose by 19% to $548.5 million in 2025.

rw.headline: Equity Bank Rwanda launches EMMA wallet app
rw.dek: The digital wallet allows users to make payments, send and receive money, and save towards personal goals.
paragraphs: Equity Bank Rwanda has introduced EMMA, a new digital wallet app designed to bring banking services closer to Rwandans. The app allows users to make payments, send and receive money, save for personal goals, and access credit if eligible. EMMA connects to Rwanda’s national payment network, including eKash, MTN MoMo, Airtel Money, and other banks.

Customers can register for EMMA using an active mobile number and accepted identification, without needing an existing Equity Bank account. The app is accessible via a mobile number or by dialing *555*6# on supported networks. Many everyday transactions, such as transfers between EMMA users or to Equity accounts and payments at PWE tills, are free, while transfers to other banks cost RWF 20.

At the November 5 launch in Kigali, Managing Director Hannington Namara stated that while Rwanda has progressed in money movement, the next step is ensuring access improves lives. He noted FinScope 2024 data showing 96% of Rwandan adults are financially included, with 22% holding bank accounts. Namara emphasized EMMA's success will be measured by active use and saving habits, not just downloads.

rw.headline: Earthquake shakes homes across Rwanda
rw.dek: Tremors felt in Kayonza, Nyagatare, Rwamagana, Ngoma and Kirehe districts after 5.1 magnitude quake
paragraphs: Residents in several parts of Rwanda felt their houses shaking on Thursday, November 5, following an earthquake with a magnitude of 5.1. The European-Mediterranean Seismological Centre (EMSC) reported the epicentre was near Ushirombo, Tanzania. Tremors were felt across the region, including in Kigali.

Five residents confirmed experiencing the tremors, with some reporting their motorcycles and market stalls shaking. Baraka Murenzi, a motorcycle taxi operator in Kayonza District, Eastern Province, described feeling his motorcycle shake while receiving payment. Mukamurenzi Beatrice in Rwamagana said market stalls shook beneath people.

The Rwanda Seismic Monitor (RMB) stated that no damage had been reported following the earthquake. Other residents in Kayonza, Nyagatare, Rwamagana, Ngoma, and Kirehe also reported experiencing shaking inside their homes.

st.headline: Coimbra festival highlights Sao Tome and Principe culture
st.dek: The Artes à Solta festival in Coimbra, Portugal, from November 13-15 will showcase Sao Tomean theatre, dance, and heritage.
paragraphs: The city of Coimbra, Portugal, will host the Artes à Solta festival from November 13 to 15, dedicating its second edition to the heritage and culture of Sao Tome and Principe. The event will feature traditional Sao Tomean theatre, known as tchiloli, and the popular dance bulawê. Organizers announced the festival's focus on the island nation after its first edition highlighted Cape Verde.

Diogo Coelho, executive director of Golden Skill, the company organizing the initiative, stated that the festival will include conferences on Sao Tome and Principe's historic plantations, called roças, and its biosphere reserve. Musician Hector Costa will present a conference on tchiloli, followed by a concert exploring the archipelago's sounds. The Sao Tome and Principe Embassy in Portugal is partnering with the festival.

Ambassador Esterline Gonçalves Género of Sao Tome and Principe in Portugal attended the press conference, viewing the festival as an opportunity to promote the country's culture and heritage. The festival program, which is free to enter, is still being finalized and will be announced on the event's social media channels.

st.headline: OMS pledges continued support for Sao Tome and Principe health programs
st.dek: The World Health Organization will bolster efforts against malaria, tuberculosis, and health emergencies.
paragraphs: The World Health Organization (OMS) will continue to support Sao Tome and Principe in combating malaria, tuberculosis, and other diseases, while also strengthening national capacities for preventing and responding to health emergencies. This commitment was affirmed by the new OMS representative, Marjorie Mupandaré, after presenting her credentials to the Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Ilza Amado Vaz.

Mupandaré stated that Sao Tome and Principe is on a positive trajectory with its national public health program. She assured continued technical assistance and close collaboration with national authorities to address key sector challenges, particularly in public health and health emergency management. The OMS representative also met with the Minister of Health, Celso Matos, to discuss the country's health situation and cooperation priorities.

Key concerns include reinforcing epidemiological surveillance at national entry and exit points, especially given the threat of serious diseases like Ebola circulating in other African countries. Mupandaré emphasized the need to enhance the surveillance capabilities at airports and to improve the skills of health professionals in Sao Tome and Principe.

st.headline: Sao Tome and Principe statistics agency surveys businesses
st.dek: The National Statistics Institute is collecting data on sales and economic outlook from companies and market vendors.
paragraphs: The National Statistics Institute (INE) began a qualitative survey on Tuesday, November 3, in the Autonomous Region of Príncipe to assess economic activity and business trends across Sao Tome and Principe. The survey, which started on October 15, targets companies, shops, service providers, and market vendors to gather information on sales, product commercialization, and economic forecasts for the coming months.

Antónia Sousa, head of the INE's Economic and Financial Statistics Department, explained that the collected data will enable comparisons of commercial activity between periods, identify trends, and evaluate the business environment. The INE aims to understand if economic activities are improving, stable, or worsening, and to identify key business challenges like financing issues and the rising cost of living. 10 surveyors are involved, with eight focusing on establishments and services and two on market vendors in Bobô Forro.

The INE also maintains monthly teams collecting product and price information from businesses and services to calculate inflation. Sousa emphasized the need for collaboration from businesses and vendors for the quality and reliability of statistical data. This survey compares the first half of 2026 with the same period in 2025 and looks at prospects for the end of the year.

st.headline: Sao Tome and Principe health system deteriorates
st.dek: The health minister admitted the country is ranked second in Africa for health sector decline over the past decade.
paragraphs: Sao Tome and Principe's health sector has seen deterioration over the last 10 years, according to the Ibrahim Index of African Governance. Minister of Health Celso Matos acknowledged the poor results, stating that while some parameters have regressed, others have improved.

Matos clarified that the reported deterioration covers the period from 2016 to 2025, with his government taking office only two years ago. He highlighted a stabilization in 2025 and improvements in combating malaria, with cases reducing from over 7,000 in 2024 to four to 5,000 in 2025.

Progress was also noted in controlling communicable diseases like HIV and improving access to primary healthcare, with a goal of one doctor per health post. However, non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular accidents and diabetes are a serious concern, straining the nation's limited resources.

sn.headline: Senegal's National Assembly sets budget 2027 review dates
sn.dek: The finance commission will scrutinize all ministries between November 7 and November 16, 2026.
paragraphs: Senegal's National Assembly will examine the 2027 finance bill from November 7 to November 16, 2026. The finance commission will review all government departments during this period, with intense sessions scheduled daily. The process begins on November 7 with general considerations, including public revenue and debt, followed by specific ministries each day.

Alphonse Mané Sambou, president of the finance commission, defended the procedure after disagreements with the Ministry of Economy, Finance, and Planning. He stated the review of the 2027 budget is based on the rejected 2026 rectificative finance bill, making the figures legally inconsistent. Sambou aims for institutional dialogue to facilitate the bill's adoption.

The opposition, led by Takku Wallu Sénégal, has criticized the government's budget sincerity following the rejection of the 2026 rectificative finance bill on November 3. The National Assembly's decision to proceed with the 2027 budget review, despite these tensions, signals an intent to move forward. The opposition may use this forum to challenge the budget figures.

sn.headline: Delta Air Lines flies 1.1 million passengers in Senegal
sn.dek: The US carrier celebrated 20 years of connecting Dakar with New York and its global network.
paragraphs: Delta Air Lines marked two decades of service in Senegal on November 4, 2026, with a celebration in Dakar. The US airline has transported over 1.1 million passengers between Senegal and the United States since launching its first flight on December 4, 2006. The airline now operates direct flights between Blaise-Diagne International Airport and New York's John F. Kennedy Airport.

Ryan Bowman, Delta's international strategy general manager, stated that the 20 years represent "people, partnerships, and the bonds that have shaped our journey." Jennifer Paguada, the US Embassy's charge d'affaires in Senegal, noted the flight's importance in connecting the two countries for people, families, and commerce.

Delta also highlighted community engagement, including a 2016 paid internship program for postgraduate students and support for Junior Achievement Africa's "Innovation Camps." In 2023, an innovation camp with Junior Achievement Africa and Consortium Jeunesse Sénégal involved 69 young people developing skills through design thinking.

sn.headline: Pathé Mboup joins Senegal squad
sn.dek: The 23-year-old Stade Brestois forward previously starred in Magic System's 'Magic in the Air' music video.
paragraphs: Pathé Mboup, a 23-year-old forward for Stade Brestois, has been called up for the first time to the Senegal national team by coach Patrick Vieira. He will join the squad for two upcoming matches against Sudan in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers. Mboup, who was formed at AS Dakar Sacré-Cœur, has become a regular starter in France's Ligue 1, with nine starts in nine games this season.

12 years ago, a then 11-year-old Mboup was the main actor in the music video for Magic System's hit song 'Magic in the Air'. The video, which has over 564 million views on YouTube, featured him as a young boy wearing a yellow football academy jersey. Mboup, originally from Mbao near Dakar, makes his national team debut.

Mboup's professional journey included spells at Standard Liège and Olympique Lyonnais before playing for Pau FC in Ligue 2. He joined Stade Brestois in the summer of 2025. His performances this season, including two goals and one assist in nine league matches, have caught the attention of coach Vieira.

sn.headline: Senegal opposition vows not to block finance law
sn.dek: Takku-Wallu group president Aïssata Tall Sall urged President Bassirou Diomaye Faye to act responsibly.
paragraphs: The Takku-Wallu Senegal parliamentary group will not obstruct the adoption of the revised finance law, aiming to prevent the country's paralysis and harm to Senegalese citizens. Group president Aïssata Tall Sall stated this position on Thursday, November 5, 2026, at the APR headquarters.

Tall Sall declared a stance of "republican responsibility" while maintaining opposition to what she described as an unorthodox public finance management. She stated that while they refuse to approve a management they deem unorthodox, they also refuse to hold Senegal hostage with Pastef.

The opposition leader emphasized that political disagreement should not lead to institutional gridlock or compromise daily life for citizens. She directly called on President Bassirou Diomaye Faye to take responsibility to avoid national paralysis, particularly concerning public servant payments.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone charcoal burning causes deforestation
sl.dek: Environmental agency notes economic trees are cut, threatening food security and increasing climate change effects.
paragraphs: Pa Alimamy, 65, has burned charcoal for over two decades in Sierra Leone, a trade sustaining his family. Charcoal use is widespread in Freetown and regional towns due to limited access to electricity and clean cooking, with only 36% of the population having electricity and 15% clean cooking access.

The Environmental Protection Agency acknowledges the practice's hazards, noting that burners now cut economic trees like mango and orange. Director Paul Lamin stated that deforestation from charcoal burning is severe, as trees take long to regrow and are vital for reducing carbon space.

Greenhouse gas emissions from charcoal production and use contribute to climate change, impacting forest health and future wood supplies. The Food and Agricultural Organization estimates traditional wood energy emits 2.4 GT of carbon dioxide equivalent annually, with Sub-Saharan Africa accounting for one-third of these emissions.

sl.headline: Sierra Leone vice presidents lack succession path
sl.dek: No vice president has ever been elected president, raising questions about the current officeholder's future.
paragraphs: The office of Vice President in Sierra Leone has historically failed to serve as a pathway to the presidency. Since independence, vice presidents have been appointed to balance regional, religious, or ethnic considerations, appease party blocs, neutralize rivals, or reward loyalty, rather than to cultivate ambition for higher office.

This pattern means most vice presidents enter office without a clear succession plan or an independent political base. For example, Solomon Ekuma Berewa, considered well-prepared, lost the 2007 presidential election, demonstrating that competence in the vice presidency did not guarantee electoral success.

Samuel Sam-Sumana's tenure also illustrates the precariousness of the position; he was elected vice president but later became estranged from the president, expelled from his party, and left politically isolated.

sl.headline: Commonwealth leaders seek partnerships to unlock prosperity
sl.dek: The 2026 CHOGM in Antigua and Barbuda aims to foster collaboration between governments and businesses.
paragraphs: The 2026 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) opened in Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, with leaders seeking bold partnerships between governments and businesses to unlock prosperity for the Commonwealth’s 2.7 billion people. His Majesty King Charles III joined leaders in St. John’s for the official Opening Ceremony, which celebrated Antiguan and Barbudan culture. The summit, themed ‘Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth’, is the first under Commonwealth Secretary-General Hon Shirley Botchwey and will include direct engagement with business leaders and investors.

Leaders will focus on mobilising partnerships and investment in scalable projects addressing member country needs, including skills-building, climate finance, and green energy. King Charles III noted the global strain on trust between nations, the impact of conflict, rapid technological change, and the catastrophic reality of climate change. He highlighted the Commonwealth as an opportunity to draw on collective ingenuity to address these challenges.

Secretary-General Botchwey stated the world needs the Commonwealth spirit of finding solutions and remade CHOGM as a summit of action. She called for a new model of partnership and cooperation, discarding the old division between states and business, to address the scale of global challenges. New initiatives are already underway to mobilise investment, boost intra-Commonwealth trade, upskill young people, and expand renewable energy.

sl.headline: Choithrams legacy highlighted by Forbes Africa
sl.dek: The 82-year-old business has expanded from a single shop to operations in 27 countries.
paragraphs: Forbes Africa's October/November 2026 edition featured Choithrams, a business established in Sierra Leone in 1944, highlighting its contributions over 82 years. The company, which began as a small retail shop in Freetown, now operates five supermarkets, a wholesale outlet, an electrical store, and three warehouses in Sierra Leone.

Harish Agnani, Head of Operations, told Forbes Africa that the company expanded across Sierra Leone before entering other African markets. Choithrams also operates two local manufacturing facilities producing candies, bubble gum, and laundry soap, alongside international operations in Dubai, the UK, and India.

Beyond commerce, Choithrams supports Choithram Memorial Hospital in Freetown, offering subsidized and free treatment to disadvantaged patients. A recent medical intervention by seven German doctors, funded by the company, successfully conducted 44 surgeries without patient charges, saving them between US$5,000 and US$10,000 each.

so.headline: Somalia supreme court invalidates constitution changes
so.dek: The court ordered elections within 90 days after striking down mandate extensions for the president and parliament.
paragraphs: Somalia’s Supreme Court on Thursday invalidated amendments to the 2012 Provisional Constitution, nullifying the extended mandates of the presidency and parliament. The court ordered that elections be held within 90 days.

This ruling followed President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s dismissal of Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf and his appointment of Ibrahim Eidle Suleiman, the president’s former legal adviser, as replacement. Five Supreme Court judges delivered the verdict, stating parliament ratified the amendments after its mandate expired, lacking legal authority for such changes.
Security forces stormed the Supreme Court premises shortly after the verdict and forced the chief justice out. The opposition welcomed the judgment and condemned the government’s actions as unlawful.

so.headline: Turkish airstrike kills Somali woman in Jameeco
so.dek: Hawo Madow was preparing tea when the strike hit her village, 160 kilometres northwest of Mogadishu.
paragraphs: An elderly Somali woman, Hawo Madow, died on October 27 when a Turkish airstrike hit the village of Jameeco. The strike occurred approximately 160 kilometres northwest of Mogadishu. Five people were affected by the attack, with another young man in critical condition.

Suley Ibrahim Dhere, a village resident, stated that Turkish aircraft carried out the bombardment. He said the village had done nothing to provoke them. Hawo Madow’s husband, Nasir, confirmed his wife was killed and two others wounded, stating no Al-Shabaab fighters were present.

Hawo Madow, who left behind five children, was preparing tea when the aircraft struck. Her niece, Mumino Osman Bashow, said the villagers were struggling with drought and dismissed claims that militants were being targeted. The attack followed an ambush on a Somali National Army convoy near Jameeco.

so.headline: Somalia rejects Israeli ambassador, planned embassy
so.dek: Mogadishu calls moves in Hargeisa a violation of sovereignty, demanding reversal.
paragraphs: Somalia's Foreign Ministry rejected Israel’s appointment of an ambassador to Somaliland and plans for an embassy in Hargeisa on Tuesday. The ministry stated these actions were taken without the Federal Government's consent and are therefore "null and void and without legal effect."

Michael Lotem, Israel’s first ambassador to Somaliland, presented his credentials to Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro in Hargeisa. A ceremony was also held to lay the cornerstone for a planned Israeli embassy. Somalia maintains Somaliland is part of its territory and lacks authority for independent diplomatic relations.

Israel formally recognised Somaliland on December 26, 2025, becoming the first UN member state to do so since the region declared independence in 1991. Somalia urged the international community not to recognise steps undermining its territorial integrity and warned of heightened tensions in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden region.

ss.headline: South Sudan and Sudan clash at UN over Abyei election plan
ss.dek: Khartoum warns Juba's move to include the disputed region in December 2026 polls violates agreements.
paragraphs: South Sudan and Sudan clashed at the UN Security Council over Juba's plan to include the disputed Abyei region in its December 2026 general elections. Sudan's UN representative, Al-Harith Idriss Al-Harith Mohamed, stated the move violated agreements and could undermine Abyei's final status resolution. South Sudan's representative, Sabino Edward Nyawella Amaikwey, defended the plan, arguing the rights of the Ngok Dinka population must be considered within the context of Abyei's unresolved status.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned in an April 16 to October 1 report that including Abyei in South Sudan's electoral districts could significantly increase political tensions. The final status of Abyei has remained unresolved since a 2005 peace agreement, which planned for a referendum that has not occurred due to disagreements over voter eligibility.

The Security Council also discussed the presence of South Sudanese forces south of the River Kiir and Rapid Support Forces in the north. Sudan raised concerns over both forces and the RSF's naming of a representative to the Abyei Joint Oversight Committee. South Sudan defended its forces' deployment as stabilizing and protecting civilians.

ss.headline: South Sudan launches cancer registry
ss.dek: The new registry aims to improve data collection and analysis of cancer cases nationwide.
paragraphs: South Sudan inaugurated its first National Population-Based Cancer Registry at Juba Teaching Hospital on Thursday. The registry will help health authorities collect, analyze, and report information on cancer cases, including types, distribution, and treatment outcomes. This initiative aims to address the long-standing struggle with a lack of reliable national cancer data, which has made understanding the disease's scale difficult.

Caretaker health minister Dak Doup Bichok stated that previous cancer figures, estimated at 8,124 new cases and 5,128 deaths within five years, were modelled and largely based on data from neighboring countries. Dr. Albino Amum, Director of the Cancer Registry at Juba Teaching Hospital, explained that the registry will gather information from public and private clinics through trained staff, following recommendations from the African Cancer Registry Network.

The registry, initially based at Juba Teaching Hospital, faces challenges including limited funding, a shortage of trained registrars, fragmented health information systems, and poor communication. The initiative is supported by the World Health Organization, UNICEF, Concern for Women, and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which are providing essential equipment.

ss.headline: Aid cuts risk cholera for 150,000 in South Sudan
ss.dek: Médecins Sans Frontières warns of disease outbreaks in Bentiu and Malakal camps due to reduced water, sanitation, and healthcare services.
paragraphs: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warned on Wednesday that about 150,000 internally displaced people in South Sudan's Bentiu and Malakal camps face increased risks of cholera and other waterborne diseases.

Funding cuts have reduced access to clean water, sanitation, and primary healthcare, with Bentiu camp hosting 111,000 people facing sanitation challenges and Malakal's water supply for 40,000 people at risk. Healthcare services in Malakal have also declined after the International Medical Corps withdrew.
MSF is calling for urgent funding to maintain essential services and prevent a public health emergency, noting South Sudan recorded nearly 110,000 cholera cases and 1,970 deaths since 2024.

ss.headline: South Sudan finance minister pledges reforms
ss.dek: UK reaffirms support for financial reforms during the 104th Public Financial Management Oversight Committee meeting in Juba.
paragraphs: South Sudan's caretaker finance minister, Athian Diing Athian, pledged to improve oversight, transparency, and accountability in public fund management. This occurred during the 104th meeting of the Public Financial Management Oversight Committee in Juba, which he co-chaired with British Ambassador Rebecca Fabrizi.

Minister Athian called for fiscal discipline and efficient use of public resources to enhance service delivery, stating the committee would provide strategic oversight for tangible progress. Ambassador Fabrizi reaffirmed the UK's commitment to supporting credible public financial management reforms in South Sudan.

Updates presented included the integration of the Integrated Financial Management Information System (IFMIS) and the Real-Time Gross Settlement System (RTGS) between the Finance Ministry and the Bank of South Sudan. The meeting also covered public sector salary arrears as of September 2026 and the 2026/2027 budget estimates.

ss.headline: South Sudan dialogue ends without consensus on elections
ss.dek: Political parties challenged the government's plans for December polls, citing absent conditions for credible elections.
paragraphs: South Sudan's inter-party dialogue concluded last month in Juba without reaching consensus, as political parties questioned the government's push for December elections. Analyst Abraham Awolich stated that participants argued conditions for credible polls were absent and called for postponing the December 22 elections and negotiating a new political arrangement.

Awolich, a former managing director of the Sudd Institute, said the talks failed because the government sought endorsement of President Salva Kiir's decisions rather than consensus on the nation's future. Government representatives insisted the elections should proceed regardless of the prevailing political and security environment.

The dialogue was abandoned without publicly agreed resolutions after attempts to draft a final document without all parties' agreement were dropped. Awolich also linked tensions to the recent firing of Martin Elia Lomuro as cabinet affairs minister, suggesting it would further weaken the government.

sd.headline: Australia sanctions four Sudanese figures over rights abuses
sd.dek: Travel bans and financial restrictions target SAF and RSF leaders, plus an Islamist paramilitary group.
paragraphs: Australia placed financial sanctions and travel bans on four Sudanese individuals, including SAF Commander-in-Chief General Abdel Fattah Abdelrahman al-Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo Mousa. West Darfur governor Al-Tijani Al-Tahir Karshoum and RSF field commander Hussein Barsham also face sanctions. The Al-Baraa Bin Malik Brigade, an Islamist paramilitary group aligned with the SAF, is also subject to financial sanctions.

The Australian government stated that both the SAF and RSF committed serious human rights violations and abuses, such as attacks on civilians, torture, sexual violence, and extrajudicial killings. "Those responsible for serious human rights violations and abuses must be held to account," the government said in a statement. The sanctions were enacted under Australia’s Autonomous Sanctions Regulations 2011.

The four individuals are now subject to travel bans preventing entry to Australia, and their assets are frozen. These measures build on previous sanctions against 13 individuals under the UN Security Council's framework. The conflict, which began on April 15, 2023, has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced over 14 million people, with nearly 34 million needing humanitarian aid.

sd.headline: Syrian community leaves Khartoum as conflict erupts
sd.dek: The Syrian community, once central to Sudan's economy, departed Khartoum in April 2023 amid escalating conflict.
paragraphs: The Syrian community, whose presence in Sudan dates back to the 1870s, left Khartoum in April 2023 as fighting intensified between the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF). The conflict, which began on April 15, 2023, has led to what the UNHCR describes as the world's most devastating humanitarian crisis.

Syrian migrants, including merchants and professionals from Greater Syria, established a significant economic presence in Sudan by the 1950s. Early settlers traded goods like elephant tusks and Arabic gum, while later arrivals, including physicians, contributed to the nation's development. Their community was a central social, cultural, and religious hub until their departure.

The community's history in Sudan began with merchants from Aleppo in the 1870s, followed by a new wave in the 1900s. By the 1950s, businessmen like Nicola Malouf played a central role in the Sudanese economy. The Melkite Catholic Church on Jumhuriya Street served as a key gathering place before the community's exodus.

sd.headline: Sudan war drives fuel prices over SDG 30,000 per litre in El Obeid
sd.dek: Residents face soaring costs for water, bread, and milk as transport grinds to a halt.
paragraphs: El Obeid, North Kordofan’s capital, is grappling with severe economic hardship due to the ongoing war. Petrol now costs over SDG 30,000 per litre and diesel exceeds SDG 35,000, crippling transport and forcing many to walk. Attacks on fuel stations and infrastructure have worsened the crisis, making it difficult for residents to afford basic necessities.

Hassan Ibrahim Hassan told Radio Dabanga that fuel shortages are acute, with a gallon of petrol costing over SDG 120,000 and diesel over SDG 140,000. Milk prices have also surged to more than SDG 12,000 per litre. Drinking water supplies are failing, forcing residents to buy poor-quality water at over SDG 500 per litre.

The price of two small loaves of bread has reached SDG 1,000, consuming a large part of government salaries that do not exceed SDG 150,000. Millet costs over SDG 160,000 per keila, and meat is over SDG 50,000 per kilogramme. These high prices, combined with insufficient rainfall, raise fears of a severe humanitarian catastrophe.

sd.headline: Drone attacks kill 14 civilians in Sudan
sd.dek: Power infrastructure damaged, disrupting water and electricity supplies across multiple regions.
paragraphs: Drone attacks across Sudan killed at least 14 civilians and injured several others between Monday evening and Tuesday. Eight people died in Um Dibo, West Kordofan, on Monday. On Tuesday, four died and over 10 were injured when a drone struck a fuel station in El Abbasiya Tagali market, South Kordofan. In Ed Damazin, Blue Nile region, a woman and a young man were killed and others wounded in strikes on Tuesday evening.

The attacks on civilian areas and infrastructure prompted warnings from the United Nations and the Arab League. The Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative blamed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and its ally for the Ed Damazin strikes, calling for an end to attacks on civilians. Blue Nile governor Ahmed El Omda condemned the strikes as an assault on civilians and property.

The strikes on power infrastructure have triggered widespread power cuts and disrupted clean water supplies. The Arab League condemned repeated attacks it attributed to the RSF on energy facilities in Khartoum, El Gezira, Sennar, El Gedaref, River Nile, and Red Sea states. The UN warned that continued drone attacks on critical energy infrastructure were disrupting essential services.

sd.headline: US proposes mineral trade act for Sudan
sd.dek: The Sudan IMPACT Act would offer American equipment and expertise for access to Sudanese resources, pending progress on civilian safety.
paragraphs: US Representative Jim Baird introduced the Sudan Investing in Minerals, Partnership, Agriculture, Commerce, and Trade (IMPACT) Act on November 4, 2026. This proposed law would provide Sudan with American equipment, technology, and technical expertise in exchange for access to its natural resources, covering both agriculture and mining sectors.

The initiative aims to aid Sudan's economic recovery, but its implementation depends on the US secretary of state certifying substantial progress in halting violence against civilians and managing national resources responsibly. Republican Representative Baird stated that economic cooperation could foster long-term stability if civilian safety remains the priority.

However, legal counsel Mutasim Ali from the Raoul Wallenberg Center for Human Rights expressed skepticism, calling it "too early to speak about investments and trade" while atrocities continue. Sudanese analyst Dallia Abdelmoniem noted the gap between the bill's ambitions and the political realities, questioning if conditions could be met amidst ongoing war and a lack of unified civilian leadership.

tg.dek: The MMLK movement wants coach Patrice Neveu to apologize to a journalist within 48 hours.
paragraphs: The Movement Martin Luther King (MMLK) condemned the behavior of Togolese national football team coach Patrice Neveu towards journalist Espoir Gato of Nana FM. The incident occurred during a press conference on November 3 at Kégué stadium in Lomé.

MMLK, led by Pastor Edoh K. Komi, stated that no journalist should be intimidated for asking questions, calling such actions a destabilization attempt. The organization demands a public and personal apology from Neveu within 48 hours to the journalist, the Togolese press, and the Togolese people.

The movement also asked the Togolese Football Federation (FTF) to ensure the safety of media professionals at press conferences. While acknowledging the FTF president's regrets, MMLK insists Neveu must offer his own apology, emphasizing that dignity and respect are universal.

tg.headline: Togo pharmacists warn of TikTok abortion drug sales
tg.dek: Online accounts openly promote and sell abortion-related products, bypassing strict medical regulations.
paragraphs: Pharmacists in Togo are raising alarms about TikTok accounts openly promoting and selling abortion-related products. These sales bypass the strict medical regulations and oversight required for such sensitive medications.

A local pharmacist expressed shock after witnessing a live TikTok broadcast advertising abortion products, with the seller explaining their usage. When questioned about legal authorization, the seller blocked the pharmacist. The purchase of these specific medications is tightly controlled even within pharmacies.

This issue extends beyond Togo, as a similar TikTok account in neighboring Benin, named "Avortement 2290," led to police intervention and account closure in 2025. Operators were arrested for offering abortifacient drugs without medical qualifications or legal permission.

tg.headline: Togo health insurance branch loses 106 billion CFA francs
tg.dek: African health insurers met in Lomé to address a sector growing at 10% annually but facing significant financial losses.
paragraphs: Africa's health insurance sector, despite growing by about 10% annually since 2014, is facing substantial deficits. The first African health insurance symposium, held in Lomé on November 4 and 5, revealed that the CIMA zone accumulated an operating deficit of 106 billion CFA francs between 2020 and 2024.

The symposium, organized by FANAF and APSAT, brought together health ministers, insurance directors, and industry leaders. Participants identified causes for the losses including insufficient data for pricing, price wars, unapplied adjustment clauses, poorly managed direct payment systems, medical overconsumption, and weak controls. Mamadou Koné, president of FANAF, questioned the sustainability of promising protection that is financed at a loss.

To address these issues, a roadmap for 2027-2030 is being developed. The Togolese Minister of Health highlighted the struggle of low-income citizens who must choose between food and medical care, emphasizing the need for insurers to innovate with affordable, accessible products that cover essential needs. The minister stressed that inclusion in insurance is not charity but requires adaptation to real needs.

tn.headline: Tunisia expands remote medical consultations
tn.dek: Sfax digital hospital connects Gafsa and Skhira facilities for neurology, cardiology, and nephrology care.
paragraphs: Tunisia's Sfax Digital Hospital is increasing access to specialized healthcare by expanding remote medical consultations in neurology, cardiology, and nephrology. This initiative aims to bring health services closer to citizens, reduce travel to major hospitals, and improve patient follow-up. The Ministry of Health announced on Thursday, November 5, 2026, that several hospitals now offer these remote consultations coordinated with Sfax university hospital teams.

In Gafsa governorate, the Houcine Bouzaïane Regional Hospital has implemented remote neurology consultations in partnership with the Sfax University Hospital Habib Bourguiba's neurology department. Simultaneously, the Skhira district hospital has begun offering remote cardiology consultations, coordinated with the Sfax University Hospital Hédi Chaker's specialized department. The nephrology service at the same university hospital also provides remote consultations, allowing patients specialized follow-up without needing to travel to Sfax.

These services are organized on a weekly schedule, coordinated with the central team of the Digital Hospital under the Ministry of Health. The system is expected to gradually extend to other medical fields, with ongoing work to integrate new specialties and connect more health facilities in neighboring governorates. The Ministry of Health also aims to reduce pressure on hospitals, shorten waiting times, and lower patient travel costs.

tn.headline: Tunisia jails former tobacco boss for 18 years
tn.dek: The former head of the national tobacco and matches company was also ordered to repay over 90,000 dinars.
paragraphs: Tunis's Court of First Instance has sentenced the former chief executive of the national tobacco and matches company to 18 years in prison. The court convicted him in absentia for embezzling large quantities of cigarettes intended for sale. He was found guilty of exploiting his public office to cause financial harm to the administration and gain an improper advantage.

The court also ordered the former official to return more than 90,000 dinars to the public enterprise. The charges against him included abusing his position for personal or third-party benefit. The ruling was delivered by the criminal chamber of the Tunis court.
The former leader's conviction by default means he was not present for the trial. The Régie Nationale du tabac et des allumettes (RNTA) is the state-owned entity involved in the case.

tn.headline: Tunisia temperatures rise above seasonal norms
tn.dek: Meteorologists forecast warmer weather across North Africa, with Tunisia expecting highs up to 28°C.
paragraphs: Tunisia is experiencing an unusual temperature increase as winter approaches, with thermometers set to rise above seasonal averages across the country. Mehrez Ghannouchi from the National Institute of Meteorology reported on Wednesday, November 4, that this warming trend will affect all Tunisian regions and several other North African nations.

In Tunis, maximum temperatures are predicted to reach 25°C on Friday, November 6, climbing to 26°C on Monday and peaking at 28°C by Tuesday and Wednesday, November 10 and 11. These warmer days will be accompanied by cooler nights, with minimum temperatures ranging from 14°C to 17°C.

Seasonal forecasts for November to January 2026-2027 indicate generally higher temperatures than usual for Tunisia. The institute also anticipates below-average rainfall, particularly in the northern and central regions, a trend that warrants attention as the winter period is important for water resources and agricultural activities.

tn.headline: Tunisian man admits killing pregnant wife in Montreal
tn.dek: Mustapha Khalil Mechken pleaded guilty on November 3, 2026, to the second-degree murder of his wife, Narjes Ben Yedder.
paragraphs: Mustapha Khalil Mechken, a Tunisian living in Montreal, Canada, pleaded guilty on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, to the second-degree murder of his wife, Narjes Ben Yedder. She was 10 weeks pregnant with their first child when Mechken killed her in 2024 with 49 stab wounds, many to her abdomen. He calmly reported the crime to emergency services, stating he was angry and killed her.

The 45-year-old Mechken, who married Ben Yedder, 32, two years prior, admitted he did not want a child and was concerned about a drop in family income due to maternity leave. The prosecution is seeking a life sentence with no parole for 22 years, with the judge expected to deliver a decision next week. Mechken remained impassive during the court proceedings.

Investigators found Mechken had searched online for information regarding inheritance of bank accounts, assets, and tax-free savings accounts if a spouse dies, and also researched "burn out" and intrusive thoughts. He reportedly took two large kitchen knives to attack his sleeping wife in their bed.

tn.headline: Tunisia suspends pharmacy payments over tier-pay dispute
tn.dek: The social affairs minister ordered payments halted until pharmacies end their tier-pay system suspension.
paragraphs: Tunisia's Minister of Social Affairs, Issam Lahmar, ordered a halt to payments owed to private pharmacies on November 5, 2026. This action is a response to the pharmacies' suspension of the tier-pay system, which began on November 1, 2026, due to unpaid debts from the National Health Insurance Fund (CNAM). The minister stated payments will remain blocked until pharmacies resume their participation in the tier-pay system.

The National Council of the Order of Pharmacists of Tunisia (CNOPT) expressed surprise at the minister's declarations, warning that the situation could worsen the ongoing crisis in the medicine sector. The CNOPT stated that the suspension of the tier-pay system by pharmacies was a reaction to persistent payment delays and accumulated debts from CNAM, causing significant financial strain and threatening their operations.

The conflict's consequences extend beyond private pharmacies, potentially destabilizing the entire pharmaceutical sector, including wholesale distributors and manufacturers. The CNOPT highlighted risks to financial balances, jobs, business continuity, and the availability and supply of medicines for patients. The council called for dialogue and sustainable solutions to settle debts and ensure the sector's continued operation.

zm.headline: Zambian president assures Mandevu of development
zm.dek: President Hakainde Hichilema pledged to address water, roads, and security challenges in Mandevu Constituency.
paragraphs: President Hakainde Hichilema thanked Zambians for re-electing him and the United Party for National Development (UPND) on August 13. Speaking at a rally in Mandevu Constituency, Lusaka, he assured residents that the government will tackle the area's challenges, focusing on water supply, road infrastructure, and security. He also introduced Adrian Banda, the new Member of Parliament for Mandevu.

The President stated that his administration's post-election focus is delivering development nationwide, with water, roads, and security identified as key concerns for Mandevu residents. He emphasized water as a basic necessity requiring urgent attention and highlighted how improved roads would boost mobility and economic activity. President Hichilema also directed security forces to address insecurity caused by individuals referred to as 'junkies'.

He suggested that youths involved in criminal activities should be taken through skills training programmes to become productive citizens, noting that the enhanced Constituency Development Fund (CDF) offers opportunities for vocational training. The President urged residents to abandon violence and embrace development, promoting freedom of movement without fear of attack.

Original budget figures show improving domestic financing, with domestic revenue covering 57.1% of the 2022 budget and reaching 80.2% by 2025. In 2024, domestic revenue reached K141.1 billion against an expenditure of K177.9 billion, with a deficit target of 4.8%.

eh.headline: Dakar rally to cross occupied Western Sahara
eh.dek: The 2027 race will traverse Smara and Dajla, cities claimed by Morocco.
paragraphs: The 2027 Dakar Rally will include stages in occupied Western Sahara, organizers announced on October 30. The race is scheduled from January 9 to 23, starting in Portugal and ending in Marrakech, Morocco. The route will pass through Smara and extend to the vicinity of Dajla, both cities under Moroccan control. This marks a return to desert racing after the event's absence from Saudi Arabia due to Houthi attacks.

The French organizer, ASO, presents Smara and Dajla as "the southern tip" of Morocco, despite international rulings and the UN considering Western Sahara a non-autonomous territory awaiting decolonization. The Polisario Front has considered the ceasefire broken since November 2020, and Smara experienced projectile impacts in October 2023. The rally's inclusion of these areas follows Morocco's strategy of hosting international events to assert its claim over the territory.

This decision comes as the UN Security Council debated the territory on the same day ASO made the announcement. The rally will spend five days racing on Sahrawi soil, from January 18 to 22. Spain will briefly serve as a logistical corridor for the rally caravan on January 10 before it departs for Nador. Sahrawi people have not consented to these events taking place in their territory.

eh.headline: Morocco commits to Western Sahara ceasefire after UN mission ends
eh.dek: The UN Security Council failed to extend the 35-year-old peacekeeping mission after vetoes from the US and Russia.
paragraphs: Morocco stated on Wednesday that it will uphold the ceasefire in Western Sahara, despite the end of the United Nations peacekeeping mission. The UN Security Council could not agree on an extension for the 35-year-old mission, with both the US and Russia vetoing competing resolutions. King Mohammed VI ordered officials to protect Morocco’s territorial integrity and national security.

The UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) was deployed in 1988 to monitor a referendum that never occurred. The territory of Western Sahara is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front, which is backed by Algeria. Rabat welcomed the mission's end, while Algeria and the Polisario Front expressed regret and concern respectively. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres warned of an escalation risk.

The UN classifies Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory. Morocco administers most of the disputed area, except for a small “free zone” east of a Moroccan-built sand wall. An armed conflict between Morocco and the Polisario Front lasted over 15 years after Morocco annexed the territory in 1975, claiming more than 16,000 lives.

eh.headline: Financial Times warns of Western Sahara escalation risk
eh.dek: UN mission's mandate ends after 35 years, raising fears of military confrontation and uncertainty.
paragraphs: The Financial Times warned on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, that Western Sahara faces unprecedented uncertainty following the end of the UN's MINURSO mission after 35 years. The British newspaper reported that the UN Security Council's failure to renew the mandate, due to US-Russia differences, could lead to a larger military confrontation in a region already experiencing rising tensions and an arms race.

Ricardo Fabiani of the International Crisis Group cautioned that withdrawing UN observers from the buffer zone could trigger an uncontrollable clash from any military miscalculation. Moroccan MP Lahcen Haddad called the mission's end a "gift from heaven," believing Morocco can advance its autonomy plan without UN interference, while Sahrawi presidential advisor Oubbi Bashraya Bashir stated the Polisario Front will continue its struggle for self-determination.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres stressed that the mission's end does not negate the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination but expressed concern over intensified hostilities. The Financial Times cited Fabiani's warning that Morocco might advance into the buffer zone, potentially provoking an escalation with unpredictable consequences.

ls.headline: Lesotho launches M547.4 million airport-Mafeteng road project
ls.dek: The 64-kilometre road rehabilitation is expected to take 36 months and create temporary employment.
paragraphs: Public Works and Transport Minister Matjato Moteane launched a M547.4 million project to rehabilitate the 64-kilometre road connecting Moshoeshoe I International Airport to Mafeteng Traffic Circle. The project, awarded to Sino Hydro Corporation Limited with Mafube Consulting Engineers as consultants, is scheduled for completion within 36 months.

Minister Moteane urged the contractor to ensure quality workmanship and local community involvement, including sourcing equipment locally and allowing villages access to surplus quarry materials for their own road improvements. He stressed the importance of worker welfare and adherence to specifications, warning against substandard materials.

The road project is part of the government's strategy to enhance national road infrastructure, boost trade, and stimulate economic activity by creating temporary employment. Similar road upgrades are underway, including repairs on Masianokeng road and reconstruction between Mohale’s Hoek and Quthing.

ls.headline: Mahlala urges Lesotho to exploit local resources for jobs
ls.dek: Basotho Development Front leader Bothata Mahlala says the nation must harness its own capabilities instead of relying on foreign markets.
paragraphs: Basotho Development Front (BDF) leader Bothata Mahlala stated that Lesotho must fully exploit its competitive advantages to create jobs, rather than relying on foreign markets and outside assistance. The Quthing-born businessman and philanthropist advocates for supporting Basotho-driven projects and generating employment from the country’s existing resources. Mr Mahlala, who previously contested the Mount Moorosi constituency in 2022, formed the BDF after leaving the Democratic Congress.

Mr Mahlala believes Lesotho has the capacity to produce and export on its own terms, suggesting the nation can produce goods for the South African market due to lower production costs and wages. He also pointed to the potential for job creation through agriculture and bottling clean water for export. These initiatives, he argued, do not require external help.

The BDF leader’s message comes amid ongoing economic difficulties, including instability in the textile and apparel sector, which is Lesotho’s largest source of formal jobs. The African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) was extended to December 31, 2028, but Mr Mahlala feels the country should not depend on such agreements for its economic future.

ls.headline: Naledi Funeral Planners earns tax compliance award
ls.dek: Revenue Services Lesotho recognised the company for adhering to tax laws amid a boardroom dispute.
paragraphs: Revenue Services Lesotho (RSL) recently presented Naledi Funeral Planners (Pty) Ltd with a Tax Compliant Taxpayer Award. The award honours the funeral services company for its adherence to Lesotho’s tax laws. Naledi Funeral Planners, incorporated in 2012, operates across northern, central, and southern Lesotho, offering funeral policies and related services.

The recognition comes as the company navigates a boardroom dispute that has reached the High Court’s Commercial Division. Acting Managing Director Tšolo Seutloali stated the award reflects the company's commitment to good governance and compliance, noting that clients entrust Naledi with their money. He praised the finance department for ensuring compliance with VAT obligations.

Seutloali described tax payment as a way of giving back to the country and a testament to integrity, institutional discipline, and fiduciary responsibility. The company's operations include providing funeral services, coffins, and cashback to clients who pay premiums.

ls.headline: Lesotho U-15 team learns from FIFA World Cup
ls.dek: The national squad finished 116th out of 189 countries in Baku, Azerbaijan, in their first FIFA World Cup appearance.
paragraphs: Lesotho's Under-15 men's football team participated in the FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku, Azerbaijan, from October 24 to 30. The team, largely drawn from the Lesotho Football Association (LeFA) Academy in Leribe, finished 116th out of 189 participating nations. This marked Lesotho's debut at any FIFA World Cup event across all age categories. The squad recorded three wins and five defeats in eight matches during the tournament.

Coach Mahlomola Matšoara described the experience as a learning curve, highlighting the need for local players to improve speed, physical strength, and bravery. He noted that the eight-a-side format, played in 20-minute halves, accelerated tactical decision-making under pressure. Matšoara expressed confidence that the LeFA Academy, supported by FIFA's Talent Development Scheme since 2023, would help develop more competitive players.

FIFA has supplied the academy with a development coach, Sam Smith from the United Kingdom, to nurture players born between 2011 and 2012. Matšoara advocates for the adoption of the eight-a-side format in schools to enhance players' technical, tactical, and physical growth. The tournament exposed the team to experimental rule changes and demanding conditions, with teams playing approximately two matches daily at a high tempo.

ls.headline: Lesotho pension fund reports M2 billion returns
ls.dek: The Public Officers’ Defined Contribution Pension Fund achieved M2 billion in investment returns for the 2025/26 financial year.
paragraphs: The Public Officers’ Defined Contribution Pension Fund (PODCPF) in Lesotho achieved M2 billion in investment returns for the 2025/26 financial year. Finance Minister Retšelisitsoe Matlanyane praised the fund for its resilience against global economic shocks and for upholding good governance. The fund's assets under management increased from M14.1 billion in 2025 to M16.4 billion in 2026.

These results were shared at the Fund’s fourth Annual Member Engagement Forum, themed “Be informed, Prepare for the future, We are with you.” Minister Matlanyane noted the fund's strong performance was significant given global challenges like geopolitical fragmentation and trade tensions. She added that global equities produced double-digit returns, with developed markets, particularly the United States, making substantial contributions.

Lesotho's domestic economy experienced modest growth, supported by construction linked to the Lesotho Highlands Water Project Phase II. Government finances benefited from Southern African Customs Union (SACU) transfers and water royalties. However, underlying economic growth drivers remain weak, with limited private sector expansion and persistent unemployment impacting the textile industry, exports, and household demand.
